AboutPage.title: About me
AboutPage.metaTitle: Frontend Developer in Enschede — Natalia Karaseva
AboutPage.metaDescription: Natalia Karaseva — frontend developer in Enschede, the Netherlands. 4 years building production web applications with React, Next.js, Angular, and TypeScript.
AboutPage.heroMeta: 4 years building production web applications · Enschede, Netherlands
AboutPage.heroSummary: I build product interfaces and reusable UI systems with TypeScript, React/Next.js, and Angular — from Figma and component architecture to testing and production.
AboutPage.intro1: I have been building production web applications since October 2022: three years of Angular in healthcare, and React and Next.js today. Most of my work starts at a Figma file and ends in production — component architecture, design tokens and a shared UI library, state and API integration, responsive and cross-browser layouts, accessibility, Storybook, and unit and end-to-end tests with Vitest, Cypress, and Playwright. I like taking a feature end to end and shipping it genuinely finished: consistent with the design, true to the requirements, tested, and fast.
AboutPage.intro2: At Neolook I built the frontend of healthcare software for neonatal and pediatric intensive care, deployed in hospitals including Máxima MC, UMC Utrecht, and UMC Groningen: real-time camera monitoring over Server-Sent Events, multi-person video calls with WebRTC, license-based feature and route protection, Dutch–English localization, and dark mode. Today, at Junior Einstein, I work on a large educational platform for primary schools — not one application, but several connected products on different stacks: a webshop and content pages on Next.js, and the learning environment itself as a React SPA. I build product features and reusable UI components with MUI, shadcn/ui, and Tailwind CSS, keep the interface faithful to the design, and shape the Figma-to-React workflow the team uses to turn designs into components.

designSystem.title: AI-Powered Figma-to-React Pipeline
designSystem.imageAlt: Diagram of the Figma-to-React workflow: a button component matrix in Figma with Code Connect, and the same component in Storybook
designSystem.summary: Junior Einstein is an educational web platform for primary schools in the Netherlands. The platform is built on a shared design system and a custom component library that the team develops in-house.
designSystem.contribution: Since November 2025 I have been building the component library and product UI in React and TypeScript. When AI-assisted development became a company priority, I looked into why AI-generated components still needed days of manual fixes, and proposed a new Figma-to-React process: a three-layer token architecture, a Figma plugin that exports tokens as CSS variables, and Code Connect. Building a UI component now takes hours instead of days.

earlyMoves.title: Neolook Early Moves
earlyMoves.imageAlt: Screenshot of the Early Moves application interface
earlyMoves.summary: Early Moves is a software solution to support healthcare professionals and parents in capturing and analyzing infants movements remotely, helping to detect developmental conditions early and provide better care for high-risk or premature babies.
earlyMoves.contribution: I joined the Early Moves project at its start in January 2023, where I was responsible for building the entire frontend while other team members handled the backend. I translated Figma designs into a scalable, responsive Angular application (v15-v18) using Tailwind CSS, and implemented features such as login, video recording, and translation. I also optimized the application for mobile, tablet, desktop, and wide-screen devices and created reliable email templates.

mmcFlyer.title: Máxima MC Information Flyer
mmcFlyer.imageAlt: Screenshot of the Máxima MC information flyer webpage
mmcFlyer.summary: This project is an informational webpage created to help parents prepare before using S2S Family, the software for watching their baby in the NICU. The page provides a clear overview of the software, testimonials from other parents, detailed instructions on installation, and a FAQ section. Its goal is to make it easier for parents to understand and use the system confidently.
mmcFlyer.contribution: I developed the Máxima MC Information Flyer webpage for Neolook and Máxima MC hospital in April 2023. I implemented language auto-detection so the page can be viewed in Dutch or English. To make content management easier for Neolook team members, I used Strapi to store publicly available text for the FAQ and testimonials sections. I ensured the page works well on both mobile and desktop screens and added CSS animations to make the interface more user-friendly.

s2sPlatform.title: Neolook S2S Platform
s2sPlatform.imageAlt: Screenshots of the S2S Platform on desktop, tablet, and phone
s2sPlatform.summary: Neolook's S2S Platform is a system that brings together video and AI solutions for neonatal and pediatric intensive care (NICU and PICU). It offers different modules with specific goals: S2S Family helps parents stay connected with their child, S2S Professional supports nurses and doctors with clinical monitoring and consultation, and S2S Academic provides tools for clinical research.
s2sPlatform.contribution: Over the last three years, I was mainly responsible for developing the frontend of the S2S Platform. My work included implementing new features, pages, and components, ensuring they were responsive and reliable, and making sure the frontend communicated smoothly and effectively with the backend. As the project grew more complex, I also worked on the frontend architecture to make it scalable and maintainable. Among the features I implemented were real-time camera status updates (SSE), grid and list views for camera monitoring (for both nurse stations and care telephones), a web interface for multi-person video calls, feature access and URL protection based on license type (Family, Professional, or Academic), and light/dark modes. I collaborated closely with designers, backend developers, the solution architect, and management, working in sprints with regular demos and sprint planning in Jira.

juniorEinstein.title: Frontend developer
juniorEinstein.description:
Proactively improved the team's AI-assisted frontend workflow by identifying the gaps between Figma design structure and reliable code generation. Researched AI-ready design systems, proposed a three-layer token architecture, and set up Claude Code skills, workflows, and agents that turn Figma designs into React components.
Supported designers in adopting a more consistent design process, and collaborated with backend engineers on a custom Figma plugin that integrates brand tokens into the React monorepo as CSS variables — cutting UI component development from days to hours and reducing errors in AI-generated code.
Developed product interfaces and features for an educational web platform for primary schools: a webshop and content pages on Next.js (App Router, Server Components), and the learning environment as a React SPA — with TypeScript, Redux, and Redux-Saga.
Built reusable UI components for the shared design system — button, checkbox, switch, alert, input, and others — using MUI, Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui, and Base UI, documented in Storybook.
Implemented product UI such as product cards and filtering interfaces, with responsive layouts for mobile, tablet, and desktop.
Researched internationalization approaches and implemented multilingual support for the application.
Contributed to code reviews of both team and AI-generated code, and wrote unit tests with Vitest and end-to-end tests with Cypress to improve code quality. Collaborated across backend, infrastructure, and management teams.

neolook.title: Frontend developer
neolook.description:
Was responsible for the development of frontend interfaces for healthcare platforms used in neonatal and pediatric intensive care units (NICU/PICU).
Designed and implemented the frontend architecture for several Angular applications, translating Figma designs into scalable, responsive interfaces using TypeScript and Tailwind CSS.
Developed complex UI features including patient and camera monitoring dashboards, data tables, filtering interfaces, and multi-step forms/modals.
Implemented real-time functionality such as camera status updates using Server-Sent Events and video communication using WebRTC.
Built core application infrastructure including routing refactoring, dark/light mode, Dutch-English localization, and API integration (REST, Strapi).
Collaborated closely with backend developers and designers in an Agile environment to deliver reliable healthcare interfaces.
Solutions were deployed in hospitals including Máxima MC (Eindhoven), UMC Utrecht, and UMC Groningen.

DesignSystemPage.title: Building a scalable React design system for an educational platform
DesignSystemPage.metaDescription: Case study: how Natalia Karaseva set up a three-layer token architecture, a Figma plugin, Code Connect, and an AI-assisted Figma-to-React workflow at Junior Einstein, cutting UI component development from days to hours.

role.title: My role
role.body:
I joined as a frontend developer in November 2025. My main task was to build reusable components for the library and product UI for the platform.
Beyond that, I took the initiative on the Figma-to-React process:
role.items:
Wrote a report on where frontend time was actually going when working with AI-generated components.
Researched existing approaches: AI-friendly design systems, token architectures, and AI-first Figma-to-code workflows.
Ran experiments in Figma, in React, and with different AI models to find a setup that produced correct components on the first attempt.
Proposed the new token architecture and workflow to management and the design team, and helped implement it.

DesignSystemPage.imageAlt: Diagram of the Figma-to-React workflow: a button component matrix in Figma with Code Connect, and the same component in Storybook
DesignSystemPage.imageNote: Illustration. Product screenshots are confidential, so the image shows a mock-up of the workflow.

context.title: Context
context.body:
Junior Einstein is an educational web platform for primary schools in the Netherlands. Designers, frontend developers, and backend developers work on it together.
The designers created a design system in Figma. The frontend team built a component library on top of it in React and TypeScript, documented in Storybook.
In 2025, management set a goal to become an AI-first company. AI tools had to be used to speed up development, including turning Figma designs into React components.

problem.title: Problem
problem.body: AI generated components quickly, but the results had many errors. Fixing them by hand took frontend developers several days per component. The cause was not the AI model, but the input it received.

structure.title: No structure in Figma.
structure.text: Variables and styles were not organised into layers, so it was unclear how values related to each other.

tokens.title: No token architecture.
tokens.text: Colours, spacing, and typography were often hard-coded values instead of named tokens.

values.title: Inconsistent values.
values.text: The same colour or size could appear in several slightly different variants across components.

links.title: No link between design and code.
links.text: Figma components were not connected to their React counterparts, so AI did not know which code already existed and generated duplicates.

problem.outro: As a result, every AI-generated component had to be reverse-engineered. Developers guessed which token was meant, corrected values, and removed duplication.

solution.title: Solution
solution.body: Together with the designers and backend developers, I set up a process where the design system is the single source of truth for both people and AI.

tokens.title: Three-layer token architecture.
tokens.text: Primitive tokens (raw palette, spacing scale, type scale) → semantic tokens (background, text, and border roles) → component tokens (button background, input border). Designers restructured the Figma file around this model.

plugin.title: Figma plugin.
plugin.text: A custom plugin exports the Figma variables as CSS variables into the React monorepo. Backend developers built the plugin; I defined the token structure and output format and integrated the variables into the component library.

codeConnect.title: Code Connect.
codeConnect.text: Figma components are linked to their React implementation, so AI and developers see which component and props already exist.

library.title: Component library.
library.text: Components are styled with Tailwind CSS and the token variables. Each component is documented in Storybook with all variants and states.

aiWorkflow.title: AI workflow.
aiWorkflow.text: I set up Claude Code skills, workflows, and agents that read the Figma structure and token layers and produce React components in the project's conventions.

testing.title: Testing.
testing.text: Unit tests with Vitest, end-to-end tests with Playwright, and code review for every AI-generated component.

speed.title: Days → hours.
speed.text: Measured on the same components: before, AI generation plus two to three days of manual fixes; after, a few hours including review and tests.

errors.title: Fewer errors.
errors.text: Named tokens and component links leave less room for guessing, in AI-generated code and in hand-written code.

consistency.title: Consistent values.
consistency.text: One source of truth for colours, spacing, and typography, in Figma and in code.

reuse.title: Reuse across apps.
reuse.text: The same components are used across several applications of the platform, in Next.js and in React.

adoption.title: Adopted by the team.
adoption.text: Management accepted the proposal, and it became part of the team's process. Designers rebuilt the Figma file around the new structure.

structure.title: Structure matters more than the model.
structure.text: The quality of AI-generated code depended far more on how the Figma file and tokens were organised than on the choice of model, prompt, or AI harness.

investment.title: It is an investment.
investment.text: Restructuring the tokens and the Figma file took weeks before the first component benefited. That time had to be planned and defended.

discipline.title: The system depends on discipline.
discipline.text: It works only while designers follow the token structure. New values outside the system bring the old problems back.

review.title: AI code is still reviewed.
review.text: Faster generation did not remove code review and tests. It made them the main place where developers spend their time.
